title: Mortimer's Colorful Mess
markdown:
Mortimer Mouse kept a market stall as neat as the spines upon it. Each morning he climbed from his burrow under the old oak, pushed his spectacles up, and updated a leather ledger. Theo, a sleek ginger cat with emerald eyes that missed nothing, usually made a warm puddle of himself on a crate and watched with a flick of tail.

This year Mortimer’s whiskers quivered. Market Day was coming, and with it the Fete’s Most Tidy Stall award. He wanted the ribbon and the shiny pebbles, yes—but more than that he wanted someone to notice the quiet work of arranging stories. The fear of being a speck of dust in cheerful noise sat in his chest like a knot.

The night before, under a silvery moon, he unveiled the plan. His biggest ledger. Coloured inks: sapphire for fiction, emerald for non-fiction, lavender for poetry, charcoal for dusty pamphlets, rose-pink for talking animals. He would catalogue every book by author, title, genre, and a mole-adapted Dewey he had invented because moles, he felt, deserved decimals too. This, he thought, was the path to being seen.

As his paws danced, the market hummed. Mrs Higgins peered over her pumpkins. “My, Mortimer. A parade? All those colours. Is the Duke judging knitting, or a royal procession?”

Mr Henderson’s laugh shook ripe apples. “Looks like the circus. A safety net for acrobats. Clowns tomorrow, old chap?”

Mortimer barely heard. He was assigning sea-green to adventures by water. Theo watched the tremble in his paws and stretched. The villagers’ jokes amused the cat. They tightened the knot in the mouse.

By sunrise the stall was a tapestry of tabs and cross-references. Each book wore a coded flag. He felt a quiet triumph. The judges would understand.

They did not. The badger judge tapped a volume wearing three colours. “Remarkable,” he murmured, more sigh than praise. “What is all this for?”

“Exceptional order. The essence of tidiness.”

The owl judge, feathers the colour of twilight, cleared his throat. “Dedication noted. The system obscures rather than clarifies. A great deal of fuss for little gain.”

Mortimer’s heart sank. They moved on. He began to dismantle the masterpiece, inks mocking him. Theo padded over and nudged a small unassuming pile from beneath the encyclopedias: well-worn children’s books, dog-eared, faint crayon, the true treasures.

Mortimer looked at the faded dragon, then at Theo. He did not need a ribbon to prove the stall. He needed the stories open.

“You’re right,” he whispered. He turned to the children who had gathered. “Come here. Something special.” He sat and read. Laughter and gasps filled the aisle—a sound that outranked any judge.

Later, lists tucked away, a girl clutched a chipped fairy tale. “Thank you, Mr Mouse. This is the best book. It makes me feel I can fly.”

His whiskers twitched, not with worry. The worn covers were warm. The honour was not tidiness. It was being seen as a keeper of tales, which he had been all along, under the flags.
characters: Mortimer (methodical mouse bookseller), Theo (ginger cat friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
author: StoryGen Community
